description_full: Nomura Real Estate Holdings, Inc. operates as a real estate company in Japan and internationally. The company develops, leases, and manages office buildings, commercial facilities, logistics facilities, hotels, and other properties; develops and sells condominiums and detached houses; operates housing with services for the elderly; develops rental properties; provides Internet advertising services for housing and living assistance services; and offers consignment services for planning and management for commercial facilities. It also provides asset management services for real estate securitization, including REITs and private placement funds; and real estate brokerage and consulting, insurance agency, and real estate information website management services. In addition, the company engages in the management of properties, such as condominiums and educational facilities; provision of renovation and repair work for tenants; remodeling of condominiums and housing; and provision of cleaning services for condominiums and office buildings. Further, it participates in, promotes, and supports urban development projects and reconstruction of housing complexes; and manages fitness clubs. Nomura Real Estate Holdings, Inc. was founded in 1957 and is headquartered in Tokyo, Japan.

financial_summary: Nomura Real Estate Holdings, In is a mid-cap real estate business with a $4.5B market cap on $5.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +9% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 4% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 34%.
The company is burning through $152M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 8.5× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 7.3×.

Management returns a meaningful 5.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 37% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (1.5) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Priced near or above estimated fair value, so the margin of safety has been bid away
Interest-rate sensitivity and tenant-credit risk — cap rates and refinancing costs move faster than the 10-year leases can absorb.
Remote work structural vacancy — the post-pandemic shift to hybrid work has permanently impaired demand for urban office space across most markets.
Climate and insurance cost escalation — rising premiums and coverage withdrawals in flood/fire zones are repricing assets that the market once treated as perpetuities.

sect: Its 15% operating margin trails the Real Estate median (23%) by 8pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.74x).
It accounts for 1.6% of sector revenue and 1.2% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 146 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 87% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 15% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 194% and a beta of 0.95, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -2.51 vs 5y 0.02), so read it loosely.
Trading is thin (about $3K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
val: The price sits above its blended-model fair value of $5.12 (margin of safety -3%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 27%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Real Estate peers: P/E 9.0 vs 23.9 and EV/EBITDA 9.8 vs 16.2 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of -3.4% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.1% (vs the 8% bar).
prof: ROIC of 4% falls short of the cost of capital of 6.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.07).
It runs a 34% gross margin and burns cash (FCF margin -3%).
Earnings quality is mixed: a Piotroski score of 7/9, but cash conversion of only 0.54x.
ROE of 10% is amplified by 3.5x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 8.5x net debt to EBITDA ($1.1B of cash against $10.0B of debt), with interest covered 7.3x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.51 in the distress zone.
The Beneish M-score (-2.20) sits just under the manipulation line, so earnings quality bears watching.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.9% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 4.1% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
own: Insiders own 37.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 24%.
It returns 5.2% a year to shareholders (0.9% in buybacks and 5.3% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 12 consecutive years.
people: CEO pay is $733K, and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
